title: Abu Bakr's cousin
hook: Abu Bakr stopped supporting a relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him to forgive (Quran 24:22)
carry: wouldn't you love to be forgiven

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quraysh asked what they expected, and no blame today: Joseph's words to his brothers, carried into Mecca. Which grudge did you close? Today, a quieter forgiveness, inside one family, over money and a lie. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

A household allowance, cut off. That's where this story starts. Abu Bakr, the Prophet's friend and father-in-law, had long been providing for a poor relative named Mistah. Then a rumor went round Medina accusing Abu Bakr's daughter Aisha, the Prophet's wife, of something she hadn't done. Mistah was one of the people who spread it. When Aisha was cleared, Abu Bakr swore he would never give Mistah anything again. It sounds fair. A verse of the Qur'an asked him a question instead. Today: Abu Bakr's cousin.
screen: `AN ALLOWANCE CUT OFF.` → `A LIE ABOUT AISHA.` → `AN OATH, AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the hurt. This isn't a stranger's insult. Mistah ate at Abu Bakr's expense and used his tongue against Abu Bakr's own child. Aisha's long account of these days, in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes her weeping through the nights before she was cleared. Abu Bakr's oath is easy to understand. Second, the verse. Qur'an chapter twenty-four, verse twenty-two. In paraphrase: let those among you who have grace and means not swear off giving to their relatives, the poor, and those who left their homes for God's cause. Let them pardon, and overlook. Wouldn't you love God to forgive you? And God is forgiving and merciful. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't call Mistah innocent. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to pretend. It asks him not to let the wrong cut off the kindness. Third, the question. The verse could have simply ordered it. Instead it turns Abu Bakr around to face his own need: wouldn't you love to be forgiven? Fourth, his answer. In Aisha's account, Abu Bakr says yes, by God, he would love God to forgive him, and he goes back to providing for Mistah as before. Look back at this week: a disciple asked three times, a guard's hand taken, a village comforting another family, a verse against despair, a road out of Ta'if, no blame today. This one looks the smallest. An allowance restored. It may also be the one closest to ordinary family life.
screen: `A LIE ABOUT HIS DAUGHTER.` · `PARDON, AND OVERLOOK.` · `WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `THE ALLOWANCE RESTORED.` · then, large: `WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Think of one kindness you've quietly withdrawn from someone after they let you down. A ride you stopped offering. A text you stopped sending. An invitation that no longer goes out. You don't have to decide they were right. Just look at the kindness itself, sitting unused. Then ask the verse's question, gently, of yourself. And picture handing that one kindness back, just once. If you pray, you can bring the question to God in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Mistah. The poor relative who helped spread a lie about Aisha, and whose support was restored after a verse asked a question. Today's word.
Your line: wouldn't you love to be forgiven. Today, restore one small kindness you quietly stopped: the text, the ride, the invitation. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims read Qur'an 24:22 with the account of Abu Bakr and Mistah, and it is cited to encourage people not to cut off support to relatives who have wronged them.

myth: the verse declares that Mistah did nothing wrong
it doesn't. it asks Abu Bakr not to let the wrong cut off his giving.
the verse asks a question instead of only giving an order
wouldn't you love God to forgive you?

fork.setup: you're Abu Bakr. a relative you've long provided for helped spread a lie about your daughter. she's been cleared. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he had sworn to stop. when the verse asked, wouldn't you love God to forgive you, he said yes, and went back to providing for Mistah.

original.note: Arabic, Qur'an 24:22: let them pardon, and let them overlook.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness is a feeling you wait for.
what it means: a withdrawn kindness, restored, because the verse asked: wouldn't you love to be forgiven?
what a scholar hears: Aisha's own account of the slander, the ifk, in Sahih al-Bukhari, with Qur'an 24:22 and Abu Bakr's yes.

Bukhari 4750 (the long hadith of the ifk) for the weeping, Abu Bakr's oath and his 'yes, by God, I love that God should forgive me': confirm number and paraphrase.
